claims.statement: Developer and Developer Pro subscriptions are cloud-only restricted environments for a single developer or CI, with no backup, VPN, or SLA support, and cannot host test, staging, or production environments.

Production and test pricing includes automated backup and support for SLA and VPN, with geo-replicated backup included in cloud environments; Single compute is limited to four engines and Flexi is recommended for scalable production workloads.

The architecture overview documents both a single-machine containerized service associated with Developer/Single compute and a Kubernetes clustered service associated with Multi compute that can scale across machines.
Hosted software is distributed as OCI/Docker images in a private Docker Hub repository, and the infrastructure overview describes Terraform provisioning on Microsoft Azure.

The single-machine layout uses individual resource groups in a shared Azure subscription and managed network disks; the clustered layout uses an Azure subscription per customer and local NVMe and/or managed network disks, with a Network Security Group for each subscription.
Subscription groups share a common network, and a clustered subscription group exists inside its own Azure subscription.
In the single-machine overview, all software except the agent runs as Docker containers; the host agent self-updates, supervises the other components, and automatically upgrades them.

Both overview layouts use a TLS-terminating, traffic-managing reverse proxy on port 443 with automatically managed Let's Encrypt certificates; the single-machine layout also permits operator-provided certificates.

The single-machine node hosts the service API; the clustered aggregator hosts the service API, a storage node stores configuration and provisioner topology, a Kubernetes-operator provisioner provisions processing pipes, and execution nodes run one or more pipes.
User-defined microservices run as individual Docker containers in the single-machine overview and individual Kubernetes deployments in the clustered overview.
Both documented layouts have log shippers and metrics agents sending telemetry to Sesam for operational monitoring, with log shipping also serving billing purposes.
Sesam persists data in embedded RocksDB using MessagePack and RocksDB's default compression settings.

The overview's claim that data never leaves North Europe (Dublin, Ireland) is in unresolved scope tension with its geo-redundant backup sections and the pricing/BYOK descriptions of geo-replicated backup storage; these sources do not establish a specific secondary region or an all-copies residency guarantee.
The overview says BYOK is unsupported, but the focused BYOK feature documents support-owned opt-in setup for new single subscriptions and says multi subscriptions are not supported.

The focused BYOK reference describes platform-managed encryption of hosted disks and backup storage by default; with BYOK, Sesam manages the key and the customer can decide to revoke it, generally requiring the data to be reloadable afterwards.
BYOK pricing documentation conflicts: the feature is badged free, whereas the portal API schema says enabling byok incurs additional costs and defaults it to false.

Plan-to-topology mapping is version-sensitive: the 2022-02-11 changelog describes cloud migration and inspecting Subscription > Basics for version 1 single-machine, version 2 clustered, or self-hosted; the 2022-03-24 entry says portal-created subscriptions use clustered provisioning, and the roadmap says all cloud subscriptions now run clustered.

Self-hosted cluster support is not consistently described: the roadmap says self-hosting is single-machine only and clustering is planned, while the Kubernetes installation guide explicitly remains a subject-to-change draft and ends with support assistance for licenses, secrets, and charts.

The self-hosted guide's referenced files/env artifact is absent from the checked-in operations files directory, despite the Compose templates depending on environment variables for image tags, user IDs, and host configuration.

Self-hosted example paths are inconsistent: the guide instructs traefik.yaml but the selfcert Compose template mounts traefik.yml, certificate filenames differ between the guide and Traefik template, and the guide spells base-path concatenation differently across directory and symlink examples.

The draft Kubernetes guide contains a Sesam Helm repository URL with a duplicated https:// prefix and does not provide a complete chart installation recipe, instead directing operators needing a license and secrets to support.
Self-hosted subscriptions are required to run the latest image of their chosen software channel, which is not the same requirement as selecting the channel named latest.

Sesam's phased software channels assign weekly-prod to production two weeks behind nightly, weekly to staging one week behind nightly, nightly to development, and latest to expert development with a release for every merged pull request.
Weekly/nightly upgrades are scheduled for 00–03 CET with weekly upgrades on the night to Monday; promotions can be withheld, security hotfixes can bypass the window, and downgrades are unsupported.
The single-machine self-hosted guide recommends at least four CPUs, 16 GB RAM, and a 350 GB fast-storage data partition and requires Docker on Ubuntu >= 20.04 or RHEL >= 8, preferring Ubuntu.

Single-machine self-hosting requires a portal subscription, license key, support-provided Docker repository login, and sesam VM user; the guide's data layout uses /srv/data/sesam/node-00/data linked to /sesam/node-00/data with a documented root-disk alternative.

Sesam requires a valid license for pipes to run; the self-hosted guide stores license.key in the data directory and finishes setup by adding the node URL in the portal network tab and uploading the license.

Migration of an old self-hosted installation to Compose is documented to require backing up data first, then stopping/removing running containers and copying or moving the store and license to the configured data location.

The supplied self-hosted Compose templates use Watchtower rather than the overview's host-agent layout: they define Watchtower, Traefik, sesam-node, and Fluent Bit, with Watchtower polling hourly and targeting the node, Fluent Bit, and Traefik.

Both self-hosted Compose node configurations mount host data into /sesam/data, enforce licensing, use engine-managed microservices, select checkpoint backups under /sesam/data/backup, share external sesam/microservices networks, and expose the node through Traefik's internal port 9042 routing.

The draft self-hosted Kubernetes guide requires Kubernetes >= 1.22 and at least one worker with eight CPU cores and 32 GB RAM; its GKE example recommends a dedicated n2-standard-8 node pool labeled sesam.io/nodepool: primary, kubectl access, namespace sesam, and a 512Gi ReadWriteOnce PVC with storage class standard.

The draft Kubernetes guide supports only Azure Storage Accounts as the cluster backup backend at its authored stage, including in its GKE deployment example; its PVC requirement addresses persistence separately from backups.

Self-hosted API clients require inbound 443, which can be accessible over a local network/VPN; automatic certificate HTTP challenges require public inbound 80 from any source, while the guide allows skipping that opening for operator-provided or self-signed certificates even though selfcert Compose still publishes 80.

The self-hosted guide requires outbound HTTPS to Docker domains for image updates, Let's Encrypt when using managed certificates, Sesam domains for portal/telemetry/agent services, and PyPI domains for agent dependencies; blocking these prevents updates or renewal and disrupts portal retrieval, notifications, or billing telemetry as applicable.

Self-hosted outbound firewall openings are documented as necessary to operate under the terms of service, with domain/wildcard rules or a proxy favored over fixed addresses because CDN IPs can change.

Hosted cloud NSGs expose only port 443 according to the architecture overview, while the network-policy feature supports public-access blocking or allowlists, new-architecture proxy/per-pipe access rules, and currently unrestricted outgoing traffic; this differs from self-hosted certificate and egress requirements.

VPN is a paid IPSec feature enabled through portal Products/VPN settings using customer gateway, address spaces, and authentication details; Multi and Flexi support highly available BGP/redundant connections and custom IPSec rules arranged by support.

In the overview's single-machine Local backup scope, backups run every 24 hours and seven daily checkpoints are retained on local disk; self-hosted owners are responsible for off-site checkpoint-directory or VM backups.

The overview specifies daily Azure VM Geo-redundant backups for all Sesam-hosted Single compute subscriptions, retaining the last backup, seven daily backups, four weekly backups, and four monthly backups.

The clustered overview specifies backups every 24 hours with a simultaneous Geo-redundant copy to the Azure subscription's storage account, retaining the last backup, seven daily backups, four weekly backups, and four monthly backups.

Termination deletes subscription data and backups, but the overview's single-machine Azure-backup exception retains backups for 30 days after deletion as mandated by Azure; this retention exception is not specified for every deployment store.

In the durable-data guide's daily cloud-backup recovery scenario, the last 24 hours of writes may be lost; pull sources may supply the lost data again, but pushed HTTP endpoint data may lack an automated resend path.

Restoring Sesam to an earlier backup can replay outputs already delivered to external systems, producing duplicate side effects at non-idempotent targets; the durable-data guide illustrates this with an invoice sent after a checkpoint and sent again after recovery.

metadata.durable defaults to false; setting it true stores a pipe's data and state on high-durability disk, with the guide describing replicas and durable storage as reducing loss risk rather than guaranteeing zero loss or replay-free recovery.
Durable data is recommended for pushed inbound pipes and non-idempotent endpoint pipes, and both endpoint pipes and the share pipes feeding them should have it enabled.

Durable data is paid and the feature guide says enabling it increases durable pipes' data consumption threefold; its 2022-03-25 introduction and roadmap availability on all cloud subscriptions do not override pricing's exclusion of developer backups or establish self-hosted eligibility.
Backup restoration can make pipes out of sync; automatic reprocessing can reset/rescan or sometimes rewind when enabled, but the default reprocessing_policy is continue, not automatic.
Datasets are append-only immutable logs that append new or changed entity content after comparison with the latest content hash, and retention compaction limits otherwise unbounded growth.

Default compaction keeps two unique versions per entity for reliable dependency tracking; keep_versions must be nonnegative, zero requires a time threshold, and values below two make dependency tracking best effort with possible missed reprocessable entities, especially sink-dataset hops, for which rescans are a suggested countermeasure.

Compaction cannot advance beyond the lowest dependency-tracking offset held on a dataset, preserving history required for tracked pipes to remain correct; disabled pipes still hold it back, and the reference suggests removing long-disabled pipes or commenting out hops.
Dependency tracking inspects DTL dependencies such as hops to reprocess affected source entities when referenced datasets change, and is supported only for pipes using dataset sources.

compaction.automatic and compaction.sink default to true; sink compaction prunes incrementally as entities are written, replacing automatic dataset compaction while retaining scheduled index compaction without a dataset lock; with sink compaction disabled, dataset compaction is documented once every 24 hours.

compaction.time_threshold_hours defaults to null and sets optional age eligibility, while pump execution datasets are always time-trimmed by time_threshold_hours_pump with a default and minimum of 720 hours (30 days).

compaction.growth_threshold defaults to its minimum 1.0 for automatically scheduled compaction, and compaction.compaction_interval defaults to zero for sink compaction each pipe run; a positive interval requires that many seconds since the previous sink compaction.

Logical deletion through _deleted: true is distinct from physical history removal; dataset-sink deletion_tracking defaults to true and deletes previously existing entities not seen after a full run, while retained versions remain subject to compaction policies.
An entity's _previous field can point to a version already reclaimed by ordinary dataset compaction, so a historical reference does not guarantee the historical version is still present.

TTL delete compaction is opt-in through compaction.ttl_deletes_hours, default null; when the latest entity version is deleted and older than the TTL, all versions including the deletion marker are removed, and the 2024-11-27 changelog says recovery requires a backup still containing the entity.
TTL delete and retract processing each default to a 60-second per-run timeout, after which unfinished work resumes from its prior stopping point on the next pipe run.

compaction.retract defaults to false; when enabled and output carries $retract: true, all earlier versions in the sink dataset are permanently removed but the current version is retained, deletion state is unchanged, the operation is idempotent, and keep_versions is overridden for that entity.

Retract is irreversible according to the feature reference and affects only the pipe's sink dataset, leaving upstream datasets and external consumers unchanged; $retract can be dropped by merge sources or emit_children, and downstream pipes must both enable compaction.retract and explicitly output the field to honor it.
The 2026-04-07 changelog documents retract as implemented even though the roadmap still lists permanent history removal for selected entities as planned.

The local configuration-testing guide uses the Sesam client to drain input queues while output pipes are disabled or unable to reach real systems, and compares endpoint outputs using paired expected/<name_of_pipe>.json and expected/<name_of_pipe>.test.json files; this is configuration-output validation rather than infrastructure backup or recovery validation.
